pedagogy.summary: This is a young child's introduction to human spaceflight as a human story: astronauts are people who travel to space in rockets; humans have walked on the Moon (the Apollo missions); and astronauts today live and work on the International Space Station orbiting Earth. At 5–7 the aim is factual awareness plus wonder — knowing what an astronaut is and a few concrete, vivid things they do (float, wear spacesuits, eat and sleep in space, do experiments, look down on Earth) — not the physics of orbits or rockets. The best teaching hooks are the memorable, relatable details of living in microgravity (floating food and water, sleeping strapped to a wall, no up or down) because they make 'working in space' concrete and spark questions. It connects the abstract 'space' the child has just met to real people doing real jobs, and it seeds later topics (robots/rovers, exploration milestones). Keep explanations experiential and honest: astronauts float because they are in orbit continually falling around Earth — stated simply, not as 'there is no gravity', which is the misconception to avoid.
bestPractices: Lead with vivid, concrete details of life in space — floating, catching drifting water blobs, velcro and handrails, sleeping bags strapped to the wall, eating from pouches — which make 'what astronauts do' real and questionable for young children
Use real imagery and short clips of astronauts on the ISS and of the Apollo Moon walks; first-hand-feeling footage beats description at this age
Frame astronauts as people with a job (pilots, scientists, engineers) who train hard — supporting aspiration and countering 'astronaut = superhero' vagueness
State the reason for floating simply and correctly if asked — they are falling around the Earth in orbit — and avoid saying 'there is no gravity in space', which seeds a stubborn misconception
Anchor a few landmark facts lightly: people walked on the Moon (Apollo); the ISS is where astronauts live and work now — without a full history timeline (that is a later topic)
keyRepresentations: A labelled picture of an astronaut in a spacesuit (helmet, air, gloves) — the naming reference
A cutaway/scene of life on the ISS (floating, sleeping strapped in, eating from pouches, doing experiments)
Real photos/footage of the Apollo Moon walks and of the ISS orbiting Earth
A simple 'rocket → space → living in orbit' picture sequence
commonMisconceptions: Astronauts float because 'there is no gravity in space' (they float because they are in continual free fall / orbit around Earth — state simply, don't entrench the no-gravity idea)
Astronauts can breathe normally in open space / don't need a spacesuit (the suit provides air and protection; space has no air)
The Moon landings and living on the ISS are the same thing / happening now on the Moon (Apollo walked on the Moon in the past; the ISS orbits Earth today — no one currently lives on the Moon)
Astronauts fly to the stars or other planets routinely (so far people have only travelled to the Moon and to orbit around Earth)
An astronaut is a kind of superhero rather than a trained person doing a job (they are scientists/pilots/engineers who train for years)

learn.summary: For 5–7 year olds, introduce astronauts as real people with a job who travel to space in rockets. The aim is factual awareness plus wonder: knowing what an astronaut is and a few vivid, concrete things they do (float, eat from pouches, sleep strapped in, do experiments, look down on Earth, and wear a spacesuit to go outside), that humans walked on the Moon during Apollo, and that astronauts today live and work on the International Space Station orbiting Earth. Lead with the memorable microgravity details that make 'working in space' concrete. State the reason for floating simply and honestly — astronauts and the Station are falling around Earth together in orbit — and avoid saying 'there is no gravity in space', the key misconception to steer around.

activities.title: Explore a Space Station scene
feedback: When the child predicts the water will pour down: show it drifting instead, and explain everything is falling around Earth together so nothing lands at the 'bottom'.

If the child says 'it floats because there's no gravity', gently correct: there IS still gravity up there — it is exactly what keeps the Station circling Earth; they float because they are falling around Earth together with the Station.

For the spacesuit: 'Astronauts put the suit on to go outside the Station, where there is no air — it gives them air to breathe and protection. Inside the Station there is air, so they wear ordinary clothes.'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal annotated scene reliably surfaces the target facts reading-light for this age and lets vivid microgravity details carry the wonder. An optional lift-the-flap 'why does everything float?' can make the free-fall answer a moment of surprise rather than a lecture. Keeping the spacesuit as a separate labelled reference (worn for spacewalks) is a deliberate simplification, since inside the Station there is air and astronauts wear ordinary clothes. A fixed scene cannot be manipulated like a simulation, but it presents the concrete facts clearly for young learners.
sourceClaims: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station live and work in orbit around Earth; they appear weightless because the station and everyone in it are in continual free fall around Earth, not because gravity is absent.
Humans have walked on the Moon during the Apollo programme (Apollo 11 in 1969 and later missions); no humans currently live on the Moon, whereas astronauts continuously live aboard the ISS.

'There is no gravity in space' is a documented persistent misconception; weightlessness in orbit is due to free fall — early teaching should state this simply rather than reinforce the no-gravity idea.
learnerActions: Look at a cutaway scene of life on the International Space Station and point to or tap each part to hear one short, true fact.

Find and name the astronaut floating inside the Station in ordinary clothes; notice the floating blob of water drifting instead of pouring down, the sleeping bag zipped and strapped to the wall, dinner coming from a pouch, and the big window looking down on the blue curve of Earth.
Find a separate labelled spacesuit (helmet and gloves) and learn it is what astronauts put on to go OUTSIDE the Station — it gives them air and protection because space has no air.
Look at a rocket beside the scene ('this is how they get up there') and a real Apollo Moon-walk photo ('people once walked on the Moon').
Ask or explore 'why does everything float?' and check the answer: the astronaut and everything around them are falling around the Earth together, which is why it all floats.
activities.intendedInsight: Astronauts are people doing a job in space; living in microgravity looks surprising (floating food, sleeping on a wall), floating happens because they are in continual free fall around Earth — not because gravity has vanished — and the spacesuit is for going outside where there is no air.

activities.title: Ask an astronaut (in-role conversation)
feedback: Keep answers short, concrete and honest; when asked why things float, give the simple free-fall answer, never 'there is no gravity'.
If the child asks whether astronauts could breathe outside without a suit, answer that space has no air, so they wear a sealed suit to go outside and live in an airtight Station.
activities.rationale: A person-centred topic may be well served by a role-play voice that answers a child's own questions, intended to amplify wonder and the experiential detail. At 5–7 open dialogue leans on reading or typing, so picture-button prompts keep it accessible; it works best as a companion to the annotated scene rather than the sole source of the checkable facts.
sourceClaims: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station live and work in orbit around Earth; they appear weightless because the station and everyone in it are in continual free fall around Earth, not because gravity is absent.
learnerActions: Pose simple questions to a friendly astronaut character in role on the ISS — spoken aloud or chosen from picture-button prompts ('sleeping', 'eating', 'floating', 'the Moon') so pre-readers can still ask.
Ask what floating feels like, how they sleep, what they eat, and what they can see out the window.
Follow up with their own wonder questions and listen to short, concrete, awe-filled answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Astronauts are real people with experiences a child can ask about; turning facts into a back-and-forth conversation is intended to deepen engagement and draw out the experiential 'what it is like to live in space' detail.

activities.title: Check and sort the key facts
feedback: If the child says people live on the Moon now: Apollo astronauts walked there long ago, but nobody lives there today; today's astronauts live on the Station circling close to Earth.
If the child places the Station far out among the stars: show it orbiting close around Earth.
activities.rationale: A short picture check confirms the few checkable facts and separates past Moon landings from present ISS life. Recognition-style matching confirms recall but does not by itself require the child to construct an explanation; pair it with the 'why' discussion to surface reasoning.
sourceClaims: Humans have walked on the Moon during the Apollo programme (Apollo 11 in 1969 and later missions); no humans currently live on the Moon, whereas astronauts continuously live aboard the ISS.
learnerActions: Answer 'What is an astronaut?' (a person who travels to space).
Match astronaut kit to its job: sealed helmet → keeps in the air the astronaut breathes (the suit's backpack supplies the air), suit → protection for going outside.
Point to the picture that shows where astronauts live and work now (the ISS orbiting Earth).
Say whether people live on the Moon today (no — Apollo astronauts visited in the past; astronauts now live on the Station near Earth).
activities.intendedInsight: The landmark facts — astronaut = person who goes to space, people walked on the Moon in the past, the ISS is where they live and work now — can be recalled and distinguished.

activities.title: Playful 'life in space' and a guided float (optional extensions)
feedback: Tie each playful moment back to a fact: 'The food drifts because it is falling around Earth with you — not because gravity is gone.'
Keep any walk-through a gentle guided tour with hotspots, not a free-roam that distracts from naming what astronauts do.
activities.rationale: Hands-on dragging and a spatial walk-through add enjoyable, experiential ways to meet microgravity. They risk drifting from the naming goal, so they work as supporting extras anchored back to the facts rather than the primary teacher.
sourceClaims: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station live and work in orbit around Earth; they appear weightless because the station and everyone in it are in continual free fall around Earth, not because gravity is absent.
learnerActions: In a small drag activity, catch floating food blobs or pack an astronaut into a sleeping bag strapped to the wall, then say why things drift instead of falling.
Optionally take a gentle guided float through the Station's modules, stopping at tappable spots (floating, sleeping, eating, the window) and naming what astronauts do there.
activities.intendedInsight: Microgravity can be made playful and spatial; doing and moving through the scene reinforces that there is 'no up or down' and that astronauts float because everything is falling around Earth together.

constraints: Aim for factual awareness and wonder, not the physics of orbits or rockets; keep explanations experiential and reading-light.
State floating simply and correctly — astronauts and the Station are in continual free fall around Earth — and never say 'there is no gravity in space', which seeds a stubborn misconception.
Frame astronauts as trained people doing a job (pilots, scientists, engineers), countering the 'astronaut = superhero' vagueness.
Anchor landmark facts lightly: people walked on the Moon (Apollo, in the past); the ISS is where astronauts live and work now; nobody lives on the Moon today. Avoid a full history timeline.
Depict the spacesuit as worn for going outside the Station (spacewalks); inside the Station there is air and astronauts wear ordinary clothes. Keep the 'no air in space' point tied to going outside.
Recognition/matching checks confirm recall but do not by themselves require the child to construct an explanation; use the 'why' discussion to surface reasoning.

A fixed annotated scene cannot be manipulated like a simulation, and the conversation leans on prompts for pre-readers; treat each format as offering a different experience rather than claiming any one is uniquely necessary or more effective.
Keep the conversation's answers honest and short: space has no air, so suits (for going outside) and the Station are sealed.

Full free-fall reasoning is advanced for 5–7; the original assessment credits 'they're falling around Earth' as strong and placing the Station close to Earth as partial — treat precise orbital mechanics as beyond the target grain.

The original framed conversation and quiz as secondary to the annotated scene and tagged a walk-through and drag activity as nice-to-have; these pedagogical rankings are retained as alternatives with distinct purposes, not as claims of comparative efficacy.

probeDeeper: What do astronauts wear, and why, when they go outside the Station?
Do you think there is air to breathe out in space?
People walked on the Moon a long time ago — do they live there now, or somewhere else?
If gravity really had vanished up there, what would happen to the Space Station itself?
assess.correctAnswer: Astronauts float because they and the Station are both falling around Earth together (going round and round in orbit), NOT because gravity has vanished — there is still gravity up there. The Space Station is quite close to Earth, circling around it, not far away among the stars. Astronauts are people who travel to space in rockets; some walked on the Moon long ago during the Apollo missions, and today astronauts live and work on the Space Station as it orbits Earth.

errorPatterns.pattern: there's no gravity in space, that's why they float ('gravity stops once you leave Earth')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain there IS gravity in space — it's exactly what keeps the Station circling Earth; astronauts float because they are falling around Earth together with the Station, not because gravity is gone.
errorPatterns.distractor: They float because there is no gravity at all in space.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child attributes floating to gravity being absent up there

errorPatterns.pattern: the Space Station is far away among the stars, or astronauts live on the Moon now
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the ISS orbits close around Earth; nobody lives on the Moon now — Apollo astronauts visited in the past, and today's astronauts live on the Station near Earth.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Space Station is far out among the stars.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child places the ISS out by the stars, or thinks people live on the Moon today

errorPatterns.pattern: you could breathe in space without a suit ('it's just like being outside')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain space has no air, which is why astronauts wear sealed suits and live in an airtight Station.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child assumes there is air to breathe in space

responseLevels.gap: Says there is no gravity in space and/or places the Station out among the stars or people living on the Moon today.
responseLevels.full: Places the Station orbiting close to Earth, explains floating as falling around Earth together (gravity still present), and separates the past Apollo Moon landings from astronauts living on the Station today.
responseLevels.partial: Gets ONE of the two ideas — that the Station orbits close to Earth, OR that floating isn't simply gravity being gone — but not both.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On the Space Station, astronauts float around inside instead of standing on the floor. Why do you think they float? And is the Space Station far away out among the stars, or is it close to Earth going around it? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'no gravity in space' idea is extremely common and a child holding it says they float because gravity is gone. A child at the right grain can at least place the Station close to Earth, going around it, and sense that floating isn't simply 'space has no gravity'. The 'why' tier surfaces the belief so the teacher hears it. (Full free-fall reasoning is advanced — credit 'they're falling around Earth' as strong.)
